topics.density: What density is and how to calculate it

topics.upthrust: Upthrust, weight and the particle model
topics.submarines: How submarines dive and come back up

objectives: Calculate density with density = mass ÷ volume, and give the unit g/cm³.
Predict whether an object floats or sinks by comparing its density with the liquid's density.
Explain floating with forces: an object floats when upthrust equals weight.
Use the particle model to explain where upthrust comes from.
Explain why ice floats and how a submarine dives and surfaces.

learn.title: Brief: the 100 000-tonne question
learn.body:
An iceberg can have a mass of more than **100 000 tonnes**. One tonne is 1000 kg, about as heavy as a small car. So that iceberg is like **100 000 small cars** squashed together! 🚗 A coin has a mass of a few grams, about the same as a paperclip. Drop both into the sea: the coin sinks and the iceberg floats. 🧊 So the famous rule **"heavy things sink"** is… wrong. Totally, gloriously wrong.

Your mission: find the REAL rule, so you can predict what floats and what sinks before it even touches the water. You'll be helped (and mostly distracted) by **Sir Floats-a-Lot**, the lab cat, who keeps knocking things into the test tank. 🐈

learn.title: Density = how tightly the stuff is packed
learn.body:
Picture two shoeboxes the same size. One is full of popcorn, one is full of sand. Same **volume**, but the sand box has far more **mass** squashed into it. The sand box is **denser**.

**Density** tells you how much mass is packed into each cubic centimetre of a material. The equation is:

**density = mass ÷ volume**

Mass in grams (**g**), volume in cubic centimetres (**cm³**), so density comes out in grams per cubic centimetre (**g/cm³**).

learn.alt: A triangle split into three parts: mass on top, density and volume underneath, with arrows showing that density equals mass divided by volume
learn.caption: The density triangle: mass sits on top. Cover what you want to find and the triangle shows you the sum.

learn.title: Worked example: the coconut
learn.body:
A coconut has a mass of 600 g and a volume of 750 cm³. Does it float?

1️⃣ Formula: density = mass ÷ volume
2️⃣ Substitute: density = 600 g ÷ 750 cm³
3️⃣ Answer + unit: density = **0.8 g/cm³**

Pure water is **1.0 g/cm³**. The coconut (0.8) is **less dense than** water, so it **floats**. Coconut 1, Gravity 0. 🥥

learn.title: The three classic mark-losers
learn.body:
❌ **No unit.** "0.8" on its own can lose a mark. Write **0.8 g/cm³**.
❌ **Upside-down sum.** volume ÷ mass gives nonsense. **M**ass goes on top, like the **M**ountain top. ⛰️
❌ **"Heavy things sink."** A giant steel ship is VERY heavy and floats. It's about density, not weight.

learn.title: The sink-or-float rule
learn.body:
Here's the rule scientists use. Compare the object's density with the liquid's density:

✅ Object **less dense than** the liquid → it **floats**.
⬇️ Object **denser than** the liquid → it **sinks**.

For water, the magic number is **1.0 g/cm³**. Rocks don't ALWAYS sink: **pumice** is a volcanic rock full of tiny gas bubbles, about **0.3 g/cm³**, so it floats. Wood doesn't ALWAYS float: **ironwood** is about **1.3 g/cm³**, so it sinks. A floating rock and a sinking tree. Nature loves a plot twist. 🌋🌳

learn.alt: A density ladder with a blue line at 1.0 g/cm³ for water. Above the line: pumice 0.3, petrol 0.7, coconut 0.8, ice 0.92. Below the line: salt water 1.2, ironwood 1.3, bromine 3.12, steel 7.8, mercury 13.6
learn.caption: The density ladder: anything above the water line floats in water, anything below it sinks.

learn.title: Iron that floats?!
learn.body: Harbours use floating **buoys** made of iron to mark the safe channel for boats. Iron is about 7.9 g/cm³, so how?! The buoys are **hollow**. The iron plus all the air inside gives the whole buoy an **average density less than water**, so it floats. Same trick for steel ships: mostly air inside, so the ship as a whole is less dense than seawater. ⚓

learn.title: Why a football floats in the pool
learn.body: A football is a thin skin of material filled with air. Its average density is tiny compared with water, so it sits on top of the pool however hard you try to dunk it. Push it under and let go: it shoots up like it has somewhere to be. ⚽

learn.alt: A tank of water with four blocks of the same size: block A floats high with most of it above the water, block B floats half under, block C floats almost completely under the surface, and block D lies on the bottom. A cat watches from the side
learn.caption: Sir Floats-a-Lot knocked four blocks into the tank. All four blocks have the same volume.

rows.b: Less dense than water, so it floats on top of it

learn.title: The Dead Sea: the lazy swimmer's dream
learn.body: The Dead Sea, on Jordan's western border, is one of the saltiest lakes on Earth. Its water is so dense that people float on their backs and read a newspaper without even trying. Pro tip: don't get that water in your eyes. Ever. 🧂📰

learn.title: Tug-of-war: weight vs upthrust
learn.body:
Two forces fight over everything in a liquid:

⬇️ **Weight** pulls it **down** (that's gravity).
⬆️ **Upthrust** pushes it **up** (that's the liquid pushing back).

An object **floats** when the **upthrust is equal to the weight**: the forces are balanced, so it stays put. If the weight is bigger than the upthrust the liquid can give, the object sinks. Remember: **weight** is a force, measured in newtons. **Mass** is the amount of stuff, measured in grams or kilograms. Different things!

learn.alt: Left: a boat floating with a weight arrow pointing down and an equal upthrust arrow pointing up. Right: a stone sinking with a long weight arrow down and a short upthrust arrow up. Water particles hit the objects from below
learn.caption: Floating: upthrust = weight (balanced). Sinking: weight is bigger than upthrust.

learn.title: Where does upthrust come from? Particles!
learn.body:
Liquids and gases are made of tiny particles that never stop moving and **colliding** with anything in their way.

• **Air particles** hit a floating object from **above**.
• **Water particles** hit it from **below**.

The push from below is bigger, and the **difference** between the two pushes is the upthrust. In a **denser liquid** the particles are **more massive**, so every collision hits harder, giving a **bigger upthrust**. That's why salt water holds you up better than a pool. Think of it as being pushed by a crowd of heavier ping-pong balls. 🏓

learn.title: Ice: the rule-breaker
learn.body:
Most solids are **denser** than their own liquid. Drop a lump of solid wax into melted wax and it sinks. Water is the rebel of the class. 😎 When water freezes, its molecules lock into an open pattern that takes up **more space**. Same mass, bigger volume → **lower density**. So ice is **less dense than water**, and it **floats**.

This is why ice cubes bob at the top of your drink, why icebergs float, and why lakes freeze from the top down, keeping the fish safe underneath. The fish would like to say thank you. 🐟

learn.title: The freezer bottle disaster
learn.body: Ever left a full glass bottle of water in the freezer? As the water freezes it expands, and the bottle cracks. That's the same expansion that makes ice less dense. Physics: 1, Mum's freezer: 0. 🥶

learn.title: Submarine control: become a density DJ
learn.body:
A submarine can't change its **volume**, but it CAN change its **mass**. Around the crew's inner hull are big **ballast tanks**. 🎛️

⬇️ **To dive:** open the tanks and let seawater flood in. The mass goes **up**, the volume stays the same, so the density becomes **greater than** seawater's. Down it goes.

⬆️ **To come back up:** pump **air** into the tanks to push the water out. The mass goes **down**, so the density becomes **less than** seawater's. Up it comes.

Fish do something similar with a gas-filled bag inside them called a swim bladder. Nature invented the submarine first. 🐠

learn.alt: Two submarines side by side. The left one has ballast tanks full of water and an arrow pointing down labelled dive. The right one has ballast tanks full of air and an arrow pointing up labelled surface
learn.caption: Tanks full of water: denser than seawater, so it dives. Tanks full of air: less dense, so it rises.

learn.title: Engineer maths: big numbers in kg/m³
learn.body:
For huge objects, engineers use **kilograms** and **cubic metres**. Water's density is **1000 kg/m³** (the same as 1.0 g/cm³).

A submarine has a mass of 6 000 000 kg and a volume of 8 000 m³.
Density = 6 000 000 ÷ 8 000 = **750 kg/m³**. That's less than 1000, so it floats. 🛟

Now flood the tanks with 4 000 000 kg of seawater. Mass = 10 000 000 kg, volume still 8 000 m³.
Density = 10 000 000 ÷ 8 000 = **1250 kg/m³**. More than 1000, so it dives. 🌊

learn.title: Scuba divers are density DJs too
learn.body: A scuba diver wears a jacket called a **BCD** that can be filled with air. More air → bigger volume, lower density → the diver rises. Let air out → the diver sinks. A **weight belt** adds mass so the diver can go down in the first place. Divers practise this until they can hover in mid-water, like an astronaut in space. 🤿

learn.title: Pilots: floating in air
learn.body: Upthrust doesn't only happen in water: air gives upthrust too. A **hot-air balloon** rises because the hot air inside is less dense than the cooler air around it, so the whole balloon is less dense than the air. Same rule, different fluid. 🎈✈️

learn.title: The 3-step answer that wins density marks
learn.body:
For any "will it float?" question:
1️⃣ Give the object's density (calculate it if you need to).
2️⃣ Compare it with the liquid's density, using **more dense than** or **less dense than**.
3️⃣ Conclude: **floats** or **sinks**.
Examiners LOVE the word **"than"**. Never say "it's dense" on its own: dense compared with WHAT?

check.prompt: Sir Floats-a-Lot wants the density equation. Which one is correct?
check.hint: Density is the mass packed into each cubic centimetre. Which sum shares the mass out between the cubic centimetres?
options: density = how scared the object is of water
check.explanation: Density is mass divided by volume. Mass goes on top. (Objects don't get scared of water. We checked.)

check.prompt: A toy boat has a mass of 120 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Complete the working. Not every word is used.
check.hint: Follow the three steps: formula, substitute the numbers, then work out the answer with its unit.
check.explanation: density = mass ÷ volume = 120 g ÷ 200 cm³ = 0.6 g/cm³. 1.67 is what you get if you divide the wrong way round.

check.prompt: Sir Floats-a-Lot drops these into pure water (1.0 g/cm³). Tick (✓) whether each one floats or sinks.
check.hint: Compare each number with water's magic number. Is it smaller or bigger?

rows.explanation: 0.24 is less than 1.0, so it floats.
7.8 is more than 1.0, so it sinks.
A rock that floats: 0.3 is less than 1.0.
Wood that sinks: 1.3 is more than 1.0.

check.explanation: Two correct rows earn one mark. Compare each density with 1.0: less floats, more sinks.

check.prompt: Why does a swimmer float more easily in the Dead Sea than in a swimming pool?
check.hint: Look at the liquids table. How does salt water compare with pure water?
options: Salt water is less dense than pool water
Salt water is denser than pool water
The swimmer's mass is smaller in the Dead Sea
The Dead Sea is too lazy to let you sink
check.explanation: Salt water (about 1.2 g/cm³) is denser than pure water (1.0 g/cm³), so it gives a bigger upthrust. Your mass doesn't change when you go on holiday.

check.prompt: Complete the sentences about forces on a floating object. Not every word is used.
check.hint: Picture the tug-of-war diagram. Which way does gravity pull, and what does balanced mean?

items.sentence: An object floats when the upthrust is ___ the weight.

check.explanation: Weight acts downwards, upthrust acts upwards, and floating means they are balanced.

check.prompt: Why does ice float on water?
check.hint: When water freezes, does it take up more space or less? Then think: same mass, different volume.
options: Ice is colder, so it has no mass
Water expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense than water
Ice cubes are secretly good swimmers
check.explanation: Freezing makes water take up more space. Same mass, bigger volume, so lower density. Ice has plenty of mass: drop one on your toe and see.

check.prompt: Look at Sir Floats-a-Lot's tank. All four blocks have the same volume. Tick (✓) whether each statement is true or false.
check.hint: Same size blocks: the more of a block that is under the water, the more mass it has packed in.

rows.statement: Block A is the least dense block.
rows.explanation: A floats highest, so it is the least dense.

rows.statement: Block D is denser than water.
rows.explanation: D sank to the bottom, so it is denser than water.

rows.statement: Block C is less dense than block B.
rows.explanation: C sits lower in the water than B, so C is denser than B.

rows.statement: All four blocks are less dense than water.
rows.explanation: D sank, so D is denser than water.

check.explanation: A block that floats lower in the water is denser. A block on the bottom is denser than water.

check.prompt: Match each submarine event to what happens.
check.hint: A submarine is a density DJ. Which part of the density sum can it change, and which part is fixed?

left.text: Seawater floods into the ballast tanks
Air pushes the water out of the ballast tanks
The volume of the submarine while the tanks fill

right.text: The mass increases, so the submarine dives
The mass decreases, so the submarine rises

check.explanation: Filling the tanks with water adds mass (dive). Air pushes the water out, so the mass falls (rise). The hull's volume never changes.

check.prompt: Engineer maths: a submarine has a mass of 4 000 000 kg and a volume of 5 000 m³. Seawater is about 1000 kg/m³. Complete the working. Not every word is used.
check.hint: Same three steps as always, just bigger numbers: mass on top, volume underneath, then compare with seawater.

items.sentence: 800 is less than 1000, so the submarine will ___.

check.explanation: 4 000 000 ÷ 5 000 = 800 kg/m³. That's less dense than seawater, so it floats until the tanks take in water.

check.prompt: Exam skills! A ball has a density of 1.5 g/cm³. Which answer would get FULL marks for 'Will it float in water? Explain.'
check.hint: Check each answer for a decision AND a comparison of two densities.
options: It sinks because it is heavy.
It sinks because its density (1.5 g/cm³) is greater than water's density (1.0 g/cm³).
It floats because it is dense.
It sinks because Sir Floats-a-Lot said so.
check.explanation: The winning answer gives the decision AND compares the two densities using 'greater than'. 'Heavy' is the classic trap.

practice.prompt: A stone has a mass of 260 g and a volume of 100 cm³. Calculate its density. Show your working and give the unit.

markPoints.point: Correct formula or substitution (density = mass ÷ volume, or 260 ÷ 100)

practice.modelAnswer: density = mass ÷ volume = 260 g ÷ 100 cm³ = 2.6 g/cm³
practice.explanation: Formula, substitute, answer with unit. If you got 0.38, you divided volume by mass: flip it.

practice.prompt: The stone in the last question has a density of 2.6 g/cm³. Will it float or sink in water? Explain your answer.

markPoints.point: Its density (2.6 g/cm³) is greater than water's density (1.0 g/cm³)
accept: greater than the density of water
more than the density of water
higher than the density of water
bigger than the density of water

practice.modelAnswer: It sinks, because its density (2.6 g/cm³) is greater than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³).
practice.explanation: Always compare: object density THAN liquid density. 2.6 is more than 1.0, so it sinks.

practice.prompt: Explain why a person floats more easily in the Dead Sea than in a swimming pool.

markPoints.point: Salt water / the Dead Sea is denser than pool (pure) water
accept: salt water has a higher density
salt water has a greater density

markPoints.point: So there is a bigger upthrust (its more massive particles push harder)

practice.modelAnswer: Salt water is denser than the pure water in a pool, so it gives a bigger upthrust on the person.
practice.explanation: Two links: denser liquid → bigger upthrust.

practice.prompt: Explain how a submarine uses its ballast tanks to dive below the surface. Use ideas about density in your answer.

markPoints.point: Water is let into / fills the ballast tanks
The mass of the submarine increases (volume stays the same)
Its density becomes greater than the density of (sea)water, so it sinks

practice.modelAnswer: The ballast tanks are filled with seawater. This increases the submarine's mass while its volume stays the same, so its density becomes greater than the density of the seawater and it sinks.
practice.explanation: Chain of three: water in → mass up → density more than water → dives.

practice.prompt: Explain why ice floats on water.

markPoints.point: Water expands / takes up more space / volume increases when it freezes
So ice is less dense than (liquid) water

practice.modelAnswer: When water freezes it expands, so the same mass takes up more volume. This makes ice less dense than water, so it floats.
practice.explanation: Expands → less dense → floats. (Colder does not mean lighter.)

practice.prompt: Use the particle model to explain where the upthrust on a floating object comes from.

markPoints.point: Particles of the liquid (and air) collide with / hit the object
Water particles hit it from below and air particles hit it from above
The force from below is bigger, so the difference in forces pushes it up

practice.modelAnswer: Particles in the water and the air keep colliding with the object. Water particles collide with it from below and air particles from above. The force from the water particles is bigger, and the difference between the two forces is the upthrust.
practice.explanation: Collisions → from below (water) and above (air) → the difference is the upthrust.

practice.prompt: State, in terms of forces, when an object floats.

markPoints.point: When the upthrust is equal to the weight

practice.modelAnswer: An object floats when the upthrust on it is equal to its weight.

summary: density = mass ÷ volume. With grams and cm³, the unit is g/cm³.
Less dense than the liquid → floats. Denser than the liquid → sinks. Water = 1.0 g/cm³.
Some rocks float (pumice) and some wood sinks (ironwood). Hollow iron buoys and steel ships float because their average density is less than water.
An object floats when upthrust = weight. Particles hitting from below push harder than those from above: the difference is upthrust.
A denser liquid (like salt water) has more massive particles, so it gives a bigger upthrust.
Ice floats because water expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense than water.
Submarines: water into the ballast tanks → mass up → denser than seawater → dive. Air in, water out → less dense → rise.
